speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I would, first and foremost, like to salute our healthcare workers for their immense contribution to our nation and for all the sacrifices they have made to help our country overcome the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We owe them a debt of gratitude for putting themselves out in the frontlines, and I hope that we, as a nation, will continue to appreciate their service.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Our healthcare system has delivered good outcomes overall to date.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, there is still further room for improvement.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We owe it to our nation, our constituents, our families and indeed ourselves to continually seek ways to improve Singapore's healthcare system, because all of us may become patients at one time or another in our life.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The central theme of my speech today is to ensure that patients' interests are protected within our healthcare system.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In preparing for this speech, my colleagues and I in the Workers' Party consulted insurers, hospital administrators, insurance agents, doctors in both private and public practice, and constituents to better understand their concerns and hear their perspectives on the issues.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I recognise that the cost of healthcare is an enormous topic, of which I will only be able to scratch the surface in the time I have today for my speech.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I will, therefore, focus on just three areas: medical fee benchmarks, health insurance coverage and over-servicing of healthcare.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In each of these areas, I will suggest policy changes which I believe will benefit patients over the long term.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In 1987, the Singapore Medical Association or SMA first issued their Guidelines on Fees or GOF.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The GOF was issued in response to complaints of overcharging made by members of the public against doctors.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: SMA's stated objective was to provide greater transparency of medical fees and safeguard the interests of patients.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Unfortunately, the GOF was withdrawn in 2007 after being flagged as being potentially anti-competitive.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In its 2010 decision on the matter, the Competition Commission of Singapore (CCS) advised SMA that the GOF would contravene the section 34 prohibition of the Competition Act.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While acknowledging that the GOF was an attempt to address information asymmetry in the medical sector, CCS at that time said that there were "other more effective measures'' in place.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, with nothing to immediately supersede the GOF, the longer term impact of its revocation on medical costs may have been even worse than the initial problem the CCS was trying to correct.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To be clear, there were other factors beyond the removal of the GOF that led to rising healthcare costs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The removal of the GOF coincided with the expansion of zero payment "full riders" for MediShield Integrated Shield Plans or IPs and a rapid increase in rents in private hospitals.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This trio of changes could have created a perfect storm which accounts for much of the rapid growth in healthcare costs in the private sector.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: But it was not until January 2018 that the Fee Benchmarks Advisory Committee or FBAC was appointed by MOH to set reasonable Fee Benchmarks for surgical procedures and services.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The FBAC came out with its first set of benchmarks in November 2018.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Why did it take MOH more than 10 years to replace the GOF with its own Fee Benchmarks?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Had the Fee Benchmarks been introduced soon after the revocation of the GOF, we might not have seen such a steep healthcare cost inflation over that decade.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, I am glad we now have the Fee Benchmarks to work with.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: According to the FBAC, the Fee Benchmarks are intended as a common reference for all stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Doctors can use them to set fair and appropriate fees.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Insurers can use them to manage and assess claims.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And patients can use the benchmarks to discuss with their doctors about their condition, available treatment options and fees.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Fee Benchmarks, therefore, have an outsize influence on the fees doctors charge, and the premiums, payouts and coverage of health insurance.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: By providing more transparency on doctors' fees, they can help narrow the perennial problem in healthcare: information asymmetry between patients, doctors and insurers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, to be effective in helping stakeholders manage costs better, the Fee Benchmarks need to be more comprehensive.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Fee Benchmarks were developed based on actual fee data derived from cases of Singaporean patients submitted by private healthcare providers in a single year – the year 2017.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To do this, the FBAC could use data from several more years of MediSave and MediShield claims from private hospitals.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For procedures with insufficient transacted data, MOH could consult specialists, insurers and patients, before independently deciding on a reasonable range of fees.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Currently, the lower and upper bound of the fee range is set at around the 25th and 75th percentile respectively of the fees for that surgical procedure.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Based on feedback I gathered from doctors and insurers, this might be too wide a range to take effective reference from.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It may be more useful to set the Fee Benchmarks to a narrower 40th to 60th percentile of each fee range.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While coming up with the fee benchmarks for all surgical procedures will be a resource-intensive undertaking for the FBAC and its secretariat, it would be well worth the time and effort as it will reduce ambiguity in fees and claims for all stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It will also cut down administrative costs in the long run and reduce the need to have exclusive panels of doctors and pre-authorisation of medical procedures by insurers, which I will speak about next.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: IP insurers currently have panels of doctors that their policyholders have to choose from in order to benefit from greater coverage and lower co-payments for procedures.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: One of my constituents likened panels to an umbrella she carries to prepare for a rainy day, but when it pours, she still gets wet because of the holes in the umbrella.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: SMA has argued that panels should be expanded, while the Life Insurance Association has warned that if the number of doctors on panels is "recklessly" increased, premiums will "rise significantly".

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Doctors with an adverse track record with the Singapore Medical Council can still be excluded from the panels.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They should not use their own panel doctors' fee schedules, which may tend towards the lower end of the Fee Benchmarks.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If a doctor charges more than the upper end of the Fee Benchmarks for a procedure, he or she will need to provide written justification or inform their patient beforehand of potential out-of-pocket expenses.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Government has to take the lead in introducing these changes across the board for all doctors and insurers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: No insurer will be willing to be the first mover on this because of competitive pressures.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Insurers also cannot coordinate these changes among themselves, lest it be deemed anti-competitive.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Greater certainty of fees may lessen the need for pre-authorisation by insurers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The main reason why insurers require pre-authorisation is to mitigate the risk of over-servicing and overcharging by non-panel doctors.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, insurance companies are not in a position to decide on the medical necessity of a treatment, since they would not have personally examined the patient or understood their case history.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These are professional decisions best made by the doctor.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Even a doctor from a different specialty acting on behalf of insurers may not be sufficiently well-placed to determine if a particular treatment is appropriate for the patient.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The risk of overcharging and over-servicing should be dealt with through a different mechanism, which I will talk about next.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Every doctor is under an ethical obligation to charge fair and reasonable fees for services rendered to their patient.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Court of Appeal, in its June 2013 verdict on Dr Susan Lim vs Singapore Medical Council, said that "overcharging would constitute an abuse of trust and confidence placed by a patient in his or her doctor and this would (in turn) constitute conduct that is dishonourable to the doctor as a person as well as in his or her profession, ie, it would constitute professional misconduct." The SMC's Ethical Code and Ethical Guidelines or ECEG states that "profit motives must be subservient to treating patients in their best interests".

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The vast majority of doctors are committed to patients' best interests.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They do not view their practice of medicine simply as a trade but a labour of care and responsibility to their patients.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For every doctor that overcharges, there are many more who routinely waive charges for patients who cannot afford their fees.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: A doctor may order more investigations out of an abundance of caution, in line with their training.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Certain patients may present a higher risk of complications and therefore require further tests before arriving at a diagnosis.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In some cases, the doctor may fear being sued by their patient if they do not order sufficient tests, leading to a deterioration in their condition.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is important that we do not tar all doctors with the same brush when we accuse them of overcharging.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, overcharging and over-servicing are issues that must be addressed because they contribute to increasing healthcare costs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In doing so, we must not inadvertently create an administrative hassle for patients, insurers and doctors.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This could lead to increased costs for all parties without improvement in health outcomes for patients.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We can address concerns about overcharging and over-servicing by instituting greater price transparency in billing.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, surgeon’s fees could state the TOSP code and fee benchmark range for that procedure.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This added level of transparency will give payers and patients more confidence in the accuracy and reasonableness of bills and ensure a higher level of accountability by healthcare providers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, insurers should not unilaterally reject claims just because they deem a procedure medically unnecessary.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Doing so risks saddling patients with higher bills that they are ill-equipped to contest.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This unit must be accessible by doctors, patients and insurers to resolve disputes about fees and the necessity of medical procedures.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The arbitrators could be empowered to call upon specialists in the same field as the doctor in question to give their professional opinions on the case.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They can then decide whether to allow the charge or require it to be reversed.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: No doctor wishes to be known among their peers or patients as someone who overcharges.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The mere presence of this process will make doctors think twice before performing unnecessary procedures or overcharging.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This could make this an effective mechanism against overcharging and over-servicing, while ensuring that the quality of care provided to patients is not compromised.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Because market failure is inherent in much of healthcare, a laissez-faire approach will not drive efficiency in the healthcare system.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Government must step in and take a stronger regulatory role over the health insurance market to ensure optimal outcomes for the benefit of patients.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While I understand that there are often competing interests between doctors and insurers, I believe that these proposals can help to bridge the gulf between the two for the benefit of patients.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I hope that the MHIC, MOH, MAS, insurers, doctors, hospitals and other stakeholders will consider these suggestions with due gravity.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Ultimately, we should all share the same desire to place the interest of patients ahead of ourselves and contain the growth of healthcare costs in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Indeed, ensuring patients' interests has been and will always be a priority of MOH.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We have put in place many measures over the years and will continue to work on ensuring that all patients have access to good quality and affordable healthcare.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We have enhanced the safety net through universal coverage for life, of all Singaporeans and Permanent Residents with no disease exclusions under MediShield Life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Expanded CHAS allows subsidies for outpatient care and CareShield Life further supports long-term care for those with severe disability especially in old age.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: To ensure healthcare remains affordable and cost-effective, is an area that requires collective effort by patients, providers and insurers alike, and the Ministry works collaboratively with all stakeholders to achieve this.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Mr Gerald Giam asked why it took MOH more than 10 years to replace the Guideline on Fees, or GOF, with the Fee Benchmarks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: It is understandable, as Mr Giam is not a practising doctor, so he may not be fully aware.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: And Mr Giam has spoken to some doctors, so, I am quite surprised that he does not know, that to increase the transparency of healthcare charges, MOH had already started publishing "Total Hospital Bill" sizes for both public and private healthcare institutions in the year 2003, four years before the Guideline on Fees was withdrawn in 2007 due to anti-competition concerns.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Such transparency encourages providers to charge more competitively and enables consumers to make better informed choices about their provider.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The "Total Hospital Bill" size publication started in 2003 with 28 common conditions for the public sector and five-day surgery conditions for the private sector, using actual transacted charges.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: It was then progressively expanded to include more conditions and information.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For instance, the "Total Operation Fees" for common surgeries was published by 2014 for the public sector and in 2016 for the private sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: A further breakdown of "Facility Fees", "Surgeon Fees" and "Anaesthetist Fees" for the private sector was also made available to facilitate the comparison of private professional fees.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Today, the actual bill size publication for close to 300 procedures and medical conditions is available on MOH's website.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: While publications on bill sizes provided a form of benchmarks on charges, we decided to further reduce the information asymmetry between healthcare providers and consumers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Therefore, in 2017, MOH appointed an independent, multi-stakeholder committee to develop and recommend Fee Benchmarks for the private sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: So, it is not as if when we withdrew the Guidelines on Fees, there was a huge vacuum, there was actually a process that already preceded that, but it was enhanced and strengthened even after the Guidelines on Fees was removed and culminated in the Fee Benchmarks being promulgated.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The Fee Benchmarks serve as references for the public to assess whether the fees charged by a healthcare professional are reasonable; for medical providers and professionals to set appropriate charges; and thirdly, for insurers to take an active approach in their claims assessment and panel design.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As a start, MOH published Surgeon Fee Benchmarks for about 200 common surgical procedures in 2018.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The TOSP lists all procedures from Table 1 to Table 7 based on the level of complexity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: So, for example, a Table 1 procedure will be something much more simpler like taking out a small lump on your arm, but a Table 7 procedure will be where there is the highest level of complexity and surgical risk, involving multi-organ resections, for example.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: So, even without direct information on the less commonly performed procedures and less available datasets, doctors will generally be able to benchmark the fees based on the equivalent level of complexity for procedures codes within the same Table level.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This approach we have taken allows us to set the Fee Benchmarks for the most common procedures to achieve the intended outcome without the unnecessary administrative burden and costs of curating very limited data sets for less commonly performed procedures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This is also a point that Mr Giam has acknowledged.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: And I would like to say that our approach is far more efficient in achieving the same outcome that we want without imposing unnecessary burden on the clinicians who are busy doing their work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: And in fact, when the data set is scarce, what you have is a lot of outliers at the extreme ends which makes the range much more spread and the outliers may sometimes predominate and make the benchmarks actually inaccurate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This was also 4% higher than in the year before in 2018.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Mr Gerald Giam suggested that doctors and hospitals should be required to provide detailed itemisation of charges on their bills, to address over-servicing and overcharging.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This is in fact already required under the current existing Private Hospitals and Medical Clinics Act, or PHMCA, for hospital bills, and will be further enhanced under the new Healthcare Services Act to cover all licensable healthcare services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: On the issues surrounding Integrated Shield Plans, MOH has already implemented several measures and are continuing to explore and work on much more, which I have taken quite a bit of time earlier today during Question Time to elaborate in my response.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: And in fact, many of the questions and measures that were suggested were also brought up by the Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) Chair and many of our GPC members and backbenchers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The work by the Multilateral Health Insurance Committee, or MHIC, is already on-going on areas that Mr Giam has raised, amongst others.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: So, I shall not elaborate further and the Member can refer to my earlier Parliamentary Question (PQ) reply.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: But I would just want to highlight a couple of points which he has brought up.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: On taking a hands-on approach to regulating Integrated Shield Plans (IPs), MOH already exercises close oversight of IPs, due to their direct association with MediShield Life and also, as MediSave can be used for IP premium payments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In approving any changes, MOH considers the interests of the policyholders, as well as the need for healthcare costs and premiums to remain sustainable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As I had outlined in my earlier reply, riders are fully private insurance products, going beyond MediShield Life and IP plans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: MOH will typically not intervene in this space.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Such riders are regulated by MAS who exercises regulatory oversight on the financial viability of insurance products.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: MOH will continue to work closely and facilitate close collaboration between stakeholders to ensure that measures and solutions are put in place to uphold patients' interests in healthcare.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The Workers' Party Member's Adjournment Motion on ensuring patients' interest in healthcare focuses largely on the financial aspects of healthcare.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Lest it be construed that good healthcare is only about finances and dollars and cents, I think it is useful to remind us, all of us here, that good healthcare, is ultimately delivered by our healthcare workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Many of our healthcare workers are currently on the frontlines of this fight against the COVID-19 pandemic 24/7, putting themselves and their families at significant risk of infection and perhaps even mortality.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I want to thank them and salute their sacrifices and their bravery and their courage, and call on all Singaporeans to give them our fullest support during this period.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Let us not shun them for the job they do in this challenging and difficult time, but support them, so they can better help us.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: To all our healthcare workers on the frontline, let us remember the aphorism of Sir William Osler in the way we care for our patients: "To cure sometimes, to relieve often and to comfort always."

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Gerald Giam, you have a few minutes for clarifications.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: First, regarding the issue of the Fee Benchmarks, not containing all the TOSP procedures, for the remaining TOSP procedures which are not in the Fee Benchmarks, can the Senior Minister of State explain how are insurers who are not medical professionals expected to determine what is a reasonable fee if it is not found in the Benchmarks?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: My concern is that if they cannot find it in the Fee Benchmarks, they might either just reject the claim, or they might just take some other Fee Benchmark which may not be accurate.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I can understand that doctors may be able to find some equivalent Fee Benchmark, but I am not sure if insurers can.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: On the second point of the number of specialists on the panels, yes, I noted that he said up to 70% of specialists are already on at least one panel.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: But, if you take it from the patients' perspective, they only care about what percentage of specialists are on their own insurers' panels.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: So, can the Senior Minister of State share, for the different insurers, does he have the data on what percentage of all the specialists are on each insurance panel?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Senior Minister of State, you have two minutes.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Table 7 procedures, for example, would be usually grouped together in similar level of complexity.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And in the private sector, when we charge a Table 7 procedure, we usually kind of put the cost around the same ballpark for other Table 7 procedures.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: You can have a certain variation above and below a certain range to account for some complexity but on the whole, generally, that is the approach taken.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Even if the insurers were to try and see how each procedure can have a certain range, the fact is that the ranges will overlap, because they are all Table 7 procedures.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But if in this Table 7 codes, there are 10 procedures, of which you may have information for five, the other four may be rare and uncommon, so you generally try and place it somewhere in between one of the five.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For example, in terms of level of complexity.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, if this is a 7B procedure, it will be charged somewhere between a Table 7A and a Table 7C procedure.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: That is how you kind of get a gauge, a rough gauge.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It cannot be absolute because sometimes even a Table 5 operation can cost a bit more than a Table 7.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: If it takes longer to perform that procedure, intraoperatively there are challenges, a Table 5 procedure can cost more than a Table 7.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For panels, I think I have explained previously that it is difficult to ensure that all doctors get on panels because doctors can choose not to be on panels.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Senior Minister of State, if you can wrap up.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The time allowed for the proceedings has expired.
